questions.question: Differentiate between a primary key and a candidate key.
questions.solution_html:
• Primary key
  •  A Primary key is used to uniquely identify each record in a table.
  •  Only one primary key can exist in a table.
  •  Cannot contain NULL values.
  • Candidate Key
  •  An attribute or set of attributes that can uniquely identify each record.
  •  A table can have multiple candidate keys.
  •  Cannot contain NULL values.
  • Hash File Organization
  • Confidential
  • Stable storage
  • Short Answer Questions
  • Multivalued attribute: An attribute that can have multiple values for a single entity.
  • Represented by a double oval.
  • Billing Systems: Customer records are processed in sequence to prepare bills. Example
  • Generating monthly electricity bills. Etc
  • NULL foreign-key value: NULL is allowed if the foreign-key column permits NULL
  • values and the relationship is optional.
  • Effect on Referential Integrity
  •  Valid foreign-key values maintain consistency between the tables.
  •  Invalid foreign-key values are rejected by the DBMS when referential integrity
  • constraints are enforced.

questions.question: Classify different levels of data abstraction.
questions.solution_html:
• Different levels of data abstraction : - The three levels of data abstraction in DBMS are
  •  Physical level: Describes how data is stored in the database.
  •  Logical level: Describes what data is stored and the relationships among the data.
  •  View level: Describes only the part of the database that is relevant to a particular user.
  • Indexed File Organization
  • Unclassified
  • Derived attribute: An attribute whose value is calculated from another attribute. Example: Age
  • derived from Date of Birth. Represented by a dashed oval.
questions.final_answer: derived from Date of Birth. Represented by a dashed oval

questions.question: / users A1,A2 and A3?
questions.solution_html:
• Use GRANT options to construct a privilege-propagation scenario involving users A1,A2
  • and A3 : - The GRANT statement is used to provide privileges to users. The WITH GRANT
  • OPTION allows a user to pass the granted privileges to other users. .
  • Eg . Scenario
  • Assume user A1 owns a table named STUDENT and wants to grant privileges to A2 and A3.
  • Step 1: A1 grants privileges to A2
  • GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON STUDENT TO A2 WITH GRANT OPTION;
  • A1 grants SELECT and INSERT privileges to A2. Since WITH GRANT OPTION is specified
  • A2 can grant these privileges to other users.
  • Step 2: A2 grants SELECT privilege to A3
  • GRANT SELECT ON STUDENT TO A3;
  • A2 grants the SELECT privilege to A3. A3 can retrieve records from the STUDENT table
  • but cannot grant the privilege to another user because WITH GRANT OPTION was not specified.
questions.final_answer: but cannot grant the privilege to another user because WITH GRANT OPTION was not specified

questions.question: / recovery work.
questions.solution_html:
• Implement a checkpoint in a given transaction log and illustrate how it reduces recovery
  • work.
  • A checkpoint is a recovery mechanism in DBMS that records a known point in the transaction
  • log so that the system can reduce the amount of log information it needs to examine after a
  • system crash.
  • Without checkpoints, the recovery manager may need to scan a large portion of the log from the
  • beginning. With checkpoints, it can usually start from a more recent recovery point, while still
  • examining any earlier records required by the recovery protocol.
  • Write example of Transaction Log and write implementation of Checkpoint record into
  • transaction log . And also write how it reduces recovery work.
questions.final_answer: transaction log . And also write how it reduces recovery work
